questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to explore the French way of law studies and practice my French language at a French university. Aix-en-Provence is one of the best law faculties in France, so it was a good choice for me. It gives me a lot of opportunity to know both law and French, going further in my academic studies and furthermore career options.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Sometimes, it can be difficult to adapt to different systems/administrations. I had some hardships with the French administration, which is why I only give the experience a 9/10, but overall a really successful exchange year.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was relatively easy, as I received a lot of information in emails before my stay. However, some of the guides and other inscription explanations/information was outdated, so sometimes it could be confusing.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I attended an information meeting, where I met the other students and got both contact information for our rep at the university + general information about the exchange.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The university has reserved housing for students coming on exchange. It was as simple as saying yes to the housing offer in the beginning of the communication with the university, and then a longer process followed later. But it was generally known that had I accepted the offer for housing, I would receive it. In Aix (and France in general) they have a government organised housing for students called CROUS. We didn't have the option to choose which establishment we would receive, but all the housing options were very close to the university.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was one kitchen for 37 occupants per floor, with only cooking plates. So it was possible to cook. Furthermore, there were cheap options at university cafeterias nearby.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: That it is a very good offer, especially if you're only doing one semester. The price is very reasonable, and the facilities are okay. Furthermore, the location is great.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration for the courses was quite easy for some, more complicated for others. As I attend a university where my courses must be pre-approved, it complicated the process, as I would have to get the pre-approval and then sign the online learning agreement again, since it was mandatory at Aix-Marseille University to change the learning agreement. This was complicated be the fact that the courses at the university had changed for the next 5 year period, which made it harder to get the course contents. However, both universities were swift and the process worked out.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was always possible to contact our coordinator at Aix university. She helped us with various problems, such as getting course contents for new classes etc.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Completely successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Now it should be easier to get the courses, depending on your home institution it can vary how easy the process is. If you're required to do pre-approval I would suggest doing it in advance. However, you have 3 weeks upon arrival to change classes, which was enough time to rearrange your learning agreement etc. Therefore, it is likely it will work out with the classes you want to take.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is quite different from the classes I'm used to, to take classes where the course contents depend on your professor. In France, they don't do books like in Denmark, it is more a "cours de prof", which means that what the professor says is the curriculum.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: My classes were well suited for me. I would recommend doing most master classes, as the level might be a bit lower on the bachelor courses. I did 4/5 classes on a master level, and they were the most interesting courses. However, the bachelor classes are still difficult, as they tend to be more based on the internal legal system in France, and going in with no knowledge of this makes the bachelor classes challenging as well.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It does ressemble the lectures in the amphitheatres at UCPH, but there is a difference, which is that at UCPH you have your books and you come prepared for class for the professor to elaborate on the things in the books. At my host institution you have to come to lectures, but you don't have additional mandatory books or articles, it is solely the teachings of the professor you must know, and you must know it well. Therefore it can be challenging, since the French students go to class, open their computer, write down a dictation of everything the professor says, and then study it for the exams. As an exhange student this can be challenging in French, but I managed by listening/understanding the lecture and asking the French students for their notes, so that I could study before my exam. This went well.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Each course is 6 ects, so I took 5 classes; Droits et libertés fondementales, Histoire des relations internationales, Introduction au droit de l'environnement, Ordre juridique approfondi l'Union européenne and Criminologie.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Introduction au droit de l'environnement since it is a course that is very interesting if you're interested in green/environmental law, the French system has a lot of this in place and its very eyeopening. Furthermore, I would recommend all my classes as the professors very understandable and very welcoming towards the exchange students.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The cost of living in France is quite high, so therefore it took me a bit by surprise. There were no further costs that surprised me, as I had budgeted for insurance, transportation etc.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food in general. It is not as expensive to eat out at restaurants, but the supermarkets are quite expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a really great Erasmus network in Aix that arranges both social activities and cultural activities at a very reasonable price. Furthermore the host institution had various arrangements that were free and easy to access. The best part is the sports, as exchange students can participate in 2 different sports at the university free of cost, just as the French students can.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Doing the sports activities. Even if you're not that sporty, it can be a great opportunity to meet French students and get a new network, and since it is free it would be a shame to miss out on this opportunity.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go explore the area/region. South of France is well connected with public transportation, and it is inexpensive if you make a free bus card at the station. It's 2 euros to visit most places then. There are beautiful cities, hikes and the ocean nearby, and Marseille is only a 30 min bus ride away, with museums, shops and beaches. There are also boat rides, and the Calanques which is a must visit.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, since France is not that different from Denmark. The only thing is the politesse, which takes some adjustment. Saying "vous" every time you encounter someone/speak with your coordinator or professor.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Do sports. There is a buddy system set up to meet French students. Furthermore, they are very nice and will help you both socially and academically, so approaching them in class is a great opportunity.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Just the language was difficult at first.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food and the region with its incredible nature.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. You have to speak French or be prepared to learn. 
2. Have an open mind and practice French with the French or other exchange students - leave your English behind for the time being. 
3. Enjoy your time but make sure to attend every class as this is where you get prepared for your exams. The classes are interesting and worth your while!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress it, everything works out in the end. It may feel overwhelming at first, but there are many friends to be made and your language will improve if you put in the effort.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Improving my French and making international relationships with people from all over Europe, learning a new way of university with interesting subjects such as environmental law and finding out that I'm able to do what I put my mind up to.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language, but it improved very fast and I became friends with native French speakers so it helped me a lot.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
